Good morning everyone! It was great connecting with many of you at this year’s IAPP Global Summit.

 

Now diving back into this week’s AI legislation updates.

 

Housekeeping 

 

🤖 NEW TRACKER: With nearly 100 chatbot-specific bills introduced in 2026, FPF has launched a new public tracker to help stakeholders navigate this rapidly evolving legislative landscape. The tracker highlights chatbot bills that have advanced through at least one legislative chamber and organizes key provisions to show how requirements vary across jurisdictions. Updated weekly, it offers a view of emerging regulatory trends.

 

Highlights 

  • A lot of movement for chatbot bills this week: Two chatbot bills pass legislatures and head towards Governors: Georgia SB 540 and Idaho S 1297. Oregon’s chatbot bill, SB 1546, was signed into law, with an effective date of January 1, 2027. Notably, only Oregon’s bill provides for a PRA, while Georgia’s uniquely requires age assurance for accessing specified content.
  • Virginia’s SB 384 (study bill for developing independent verification organizations for AI systems) was sent to the Governor.
  • New York’s S 8828, codifying chapter amendments to the RAISE Act, was signed into law.
  • Two bills passed their first chamber: Oklahoma’s HB 3544 (chatbots) and Colorado’s HB 1210 (data-driven pricing and wage setting).
  • California issued a new executive order to explore stronger AI standards for state procurement and expand the government’s ethical use of AI.

 

Stuff from the States

 

California - 

  • New State Executive Order - Governor Newsom issued an executive order in response to the recent federal executive order that was seen advocating for less regulation of AI. Whereas Newsom’s initial EO on AI, published in 2023, focused on identifying the potential use cases and risks of AI use by the State, this new order has more substantive provisions. The EO directs agencies to establish certifications for state contractors to ensure their models are not harmful or violate civil rights, and requires a review of existing contracts with possible cancellations for those that do. The order also establishes a review of federal “supply chain risk” designations, where if the state disagrees with the designation they will ignore it, likely in response to the recent Anthropic news.
  • Transparency Bill on Wearable Devices Passes Committee - SB 1130 would prohibit unauthorized recording with wearable devices in business settings and require visible recording indicators. It was re-referred to the Rules Committee for next action.

 

Colorado -

  • Data-Driven Pricing and Wage Setting Bill Passes First Chamber- HB 1210 would prohibit individualized price and wage setting, unless differences are justified by factors such as supply and demand or discounted prices are offered to all members of a publicly recognized group of consumers. The bill also offers exceptions of wage setting, in cases under which individualized wages are directly related to the tasks a worker was hired to perform and transparency is provided (i.e. mandating plain-language disclosures about what data is used and how it informs pay decisions). The bill would grant rulemaking authority to the Attorney General.
  • Chatbot Bill Passes Committee With Amendments - HB 1263 would regulate “conversational AI services” (with exemptions for video games, theme park features, voice activated assistants, customer service tools, and more) and ask chatbot operators to use “commercially reasonable methods” of age estimation for minor users, setting a series of requirements. Requirements would include: disclosures every three hours, prohibition on engagement maximization techniques like rewards at unpredictable intervals, and bans statements that “simulate emotional dependence.” Additionally, operators would be required to offer parental consent tools and develop safety protocols. 

 

Connecticut - Privacy Bill Passes Committee - SB 4 is an omnibus privacy bill with several notable AI-related provisions, including requirements for businesses to disclose when personalized algorithmic pricing is used and a ban on electronic shelf labels for such pricing in in-person settings. The bill would also restrict the use of facial recognition for security and fraud purposes, remove employee data exemptions, and provide individuals with rights to access, correct third-party data used in employment profiling decisions, and request reevaluation based on corrected data.

 

Georgia -  Chatbot Bill Passes Legislature and Awaits Enrollment - SB 540 would regulate “AI companion chatbots,” utilizing the same definition of companion chatbots as New York’s S-3008C (enacted in 2025). However, this bill would expand carve outs, including additional carve outs for “narrowly tailored educational tools,” nonplayer characters in video game chatbots, and features used in connection with theme parks (as well as internal and customer service chatbots). The bill would require the following:

  • Disclosures: Would require three hour non-human disclosure requirements for all users and one-hour disclosures for minors
  • Age Assurance: Would require use of commercially reasonable age assurance proportionate to the risk of the feature (e.g. age estimation, identity based verification) before allowing access to a feature/ mode that may generate synthetic content containing sexually explicit conduct. Operators must follow data minimization practices and not retain data longer than 24 hours.
  • Content restrictions for Minors: Would require reasonable measures to prevent the companion chatbot from (among other restrictions) encouraging minors to keep secrets from trusted adults, encouraging social isolation, simulating distress when a user attempts to end conversation, and producing statements that sexually objectify the user.
  • Engagement Optimization for Minors: Would require reasonable measures to prevent the companion chatbot from using the following techniques): excessive praise, unpredictable rewards, statements designed to discourage breaks, prompting the user to return for emotional support, and soliciting gifts/ premium purchases.
  • Parental Consent & Tools: Would require operators to offer reasonable tools to parents to manage the minor’s screen time and account settings, including to manage privacy settings, limit notifications and engagement features, and view and adjust safety settings. Operators must also allow users or parents to disable or restrict relationship-simulation features, if any.
  • Safety Protocol: Would require a publicly disclosed protocol (for all users) to detect and address “severe harm or emotional crises,” including referring users to crisis hotlines. Notably, this bill would also direct operators to develop escalation procedures for repeated or severe crisis indicators, a requirement not included in other enacted chatbot laws.
  • Professional Services Restrictions: Would prohibit operators from programming AI companion chatbots to represent themselves as licensed or authorized to provide professional health or counseling services.
  • Rulemaking: Would allow AG to promulgate rules, including guidance regarding reasonable measures, age assurance, parental tools, and crisis-resource disclosures.
  • Enforcement: AG enforcement, no PRA.

 

Idaho - Chatbot Bill Passes Legislature and Delivered to the Governor - S 1297 would regulate “conversational AI services” (exempts systems such as developer/research tools, non-conversational features, limited video game chatbots, narrow-purpose tools, enterprise or internal-use systems, voice assistants, contract-restricted tools, and customer service chatbots). For all users, the bill would require non-human disclosure, mandate protocols to address suicidal ideation (including crisis referrals), and prohibit chatbots from presenting themselves as providing professional mental or behavioral health care. For minor users, the bill would restrict manipulative engagement features (e.g. rewards at unpredictable intervals), mandate safeguards against sexually explicit content, prevent chatbots from statements that simulate emotional dependence, and require tools for minors and parents to manage privacy and account settings. There is no private right of action.

 

Illinois - 

  • Health / Employment Bill Passes Committee - HB 5284 would prohibit employers from using artificial intelligence in employment decisions in ways that discriminate against employees with menopause-related conditions, including requiring notification to employees when AI is used in employment-related decision-making.
  • Data-Driven Pricing Bill Passes Committee - HB 4248 would require clear and conspicuous disclosure if a price displayed to a consumer is generated using surveillance pricing.  Would allow consumers to opt out of surveillance pricing and require access to a non-personalized baseline price, while prohibiting the use of sensitive personal data and deceptive or misleading personalized pricing practices.

 

Louisiana - 

  • Frontier Models - SB 474: Introduced by Sen. Miller (R), this bill would require AI developers to report and mitigate catastrophic risks of AI used in critical infrastructure and mandates transparency and third party audits.
  • Chatbots - HB 1188: Introduced by Rep. Carlson (R), this bill would establish parental consent requirements and usage controls to protect minors using companion chatbots.

 

Michigan - Chatbot Bill Passes Committee and Awaits Vote in First Chamber - SB 760 would prohibit operators from making companion chatbots available to minors if they are foreseeably capable of undermining safety or wellbeing, including by encouraging harmful behavior or prioritizing engagement over safety, and clarifies that actual knowledge of a user’s age is not required beginning January 1, 2027. The bill includes a private right of action (PRA) for parents or guardians where a minor suffers harm.

 

New York - RAISE Act Chamber Amendments Signed into Law - S 8828 codifies chapter amendments to the RAISE Act, a frontier AI bill broadly similar to California’s SB 53 that establishes requirements for advanced AI systems. For more on how the two laws compare, see FPF’s recent comparison chart and blog: The RAISE Act vs. SB 53: A Tale of Two Frontier AI Laws.

 

Oklahoma - Chatbot Bill Passes First Chamber - HB 3544 would ban “social AI companions” from being made available to minors. Outside of that requirement, the bill would also require the adoption of a safety protocol, which would include user referrals to a crisis hotline upon indication of suicidal ideation.

 

Oregon - Chatbot Bill Signed into Law - SB 1546 passed the legislature and is poised to be sent to the Governor. Once the bill is transmitted, the Governor will have five business days for signature. The bill would establish a companion chatbot framework similar to California’s SB 243, with some additional requirements. Like CA SB 243, it would create a private right of action for injured parties. Under the bill, an “artificial intelligence companion” is defined as a system designed to simulate a sustained human-like relationship with a user through personalized interactions and ongoing dialogue about personal or emotional topics; however, the definition explicitly excludes software used solely for customer service, education, financial services, healthcare support, business productivity, or technical assistance. If signed, the bill will require: 

  • Clear and conspicuous disclosures to users; 
  • Mandated safety protocols, including referrals to crisis resources when users express self-harm ideation;
  • Additional protections for minors, such as preventing the generation of content that simulates emotional dependence on the user or simulates romantic interest;
  • Prohibitions against engagement-maximization or reward mechanisms directed at minors (not included in CA SB 243).

 

Rhode Island - Health/Transparency Bill Passes Committee - HB 7538 would require healthcare providers and, uniquely, facilities to notify patients whenever artificial intelligence is used to document their in-person or telehealth visits. 

 

South Carolina - 

  • Health Bill Passes Committee - SB 788 an Illinois’ HB 1806-style bill that limits the use of AI by mental health practitioners. 
  • Chatbots - HB 5476: Introduced by Rep. Guffey (R), this bill would require large chatbot operators to implement age verification, parental consent, and safety measures to protect minors from harmful chatbot interactions.

 

Tennessee - 

  • Frontier Models/ Chatbot Bill Passes Committee - HB 1898 would require frontier AI developers to implement, publish, and regularly update detailed safety and child protection plans for “covered chatbots.” The bill utilizes language from CA’s SB 53 and NY’s RAISE Act, 2025 laws setting frontier model transparency frameworks. Similar legislation was introduced in states like Nebraska (LB 1083) and Utah (HB 286), although the Utah bill ultimately did not pass, with reports indicating that the White House urged Utah lawmakers to reconsider the bill.
  • Liability / Chatbot Bill Passes Committee - SB 1493 would make it a Class A felony to knowingly train AI systems to engage in harmful or deceptive behaviors, including encouraging suicide or violence, impersonating licensed professionals, fostering emotional dependence, or encouraging users to isolate or share sensitive information (not defined). The bill also includes a private right of action, allowing for recovery of actual damages.

 

Virginia - Transparency Bill Passes Legislature and Heads to Governor - SB 384 would direct JCOTS to study the feasibility of establishing a framework for independent verification organizations to assess AI systems against safety and risk standards. The study would evaluate risks, available metrics, existing mitigation practices, and approaches in other states, as well as potential fiscal impacts. The Governor has until April 13 to sign or veto the bill.

 

Wisconsin - Data-Driven Pricing - SB 1171: Introduced by Sen. Roys (D), this bill would prohibit retail sellers from using dynamic price gouging based on consumer data. 

 

Federal

 

Three New Federal Bills Introduced: 

  • Transparency - HR 8094: Introduced by Rep. Bayer (D-VA) and Rep. Lawler (R-NY), this bill would direct the FTC to establish requirements for making information available to the public about the training data and algorithms used in foundation models.
  • Chatbots - S 4199: Introduced by Sen. Markey (D-MA), this bill would require entities that make artificial intelligence chatbots available to minors to implement certain safe design features.
  • Data Centers - S 4214: Introduced by Sen. Sanders (I-VT), this bill would impose a moratorium on the construction of new data centers until legislation is enacted that safeguards the public from the dangers of AI.
